fields.Text: Core functional requirements of a news feed system include: {{c1::users can create posts}}, {{c2::users can see a feed of posts from friends/followed entities}}, and {{c3::the feed can be ranked, not just chronological}}.
Non-functional requirements for a news feed system include: {{c1::low latency feed load (e.g. <2s)}}, {{c2::high availability}}, and {{c3::eventual consistency is acceptable for feed freshness}}.

The high-level architecture of a news feed system typically includes: {{c1::a post/write service}}, {{c2::a fanout service}}, {{c3::a ranking service}}, {{c4::a feed cache (e.g. Redis) storing precomputed feed items}}, and {{c5::a graph service for friend/follow relationships}}.

Scaling bottlenecks and fixes for a news feed system: {{c1::fanout write amplification for high-degree accounts}} is fixed by {{c2::the hybrid push/pull model}}; {{c3::ranking computation being too slow at read time}} is fixed by {{c4::precomputing/caching scores and only re-ranking with lightweight fresh signals at read time}}.

fields.Front: Besides posts, what other actions typically need to be reflected in a news feed's ranking?
fields.Back: Engagement signals such as likes, comments, and shares, which feed into the ranking algorithm to prioritize relevant content.

fields.Front: Why must feed-generation latency stay low even though ranking is computationally complex?
fields.Back: Feed load time directly affects user engagement and retention — a slow feed causes users to abandon the app — so systems precompute/cache ranked feeds rather than ranking fully on every request.

fields.Front: If there are 500M daily active users and each loads their feed 10 times/day, what is the approximate feed-read QPS?
If each user has on average 300 friends/follows, why does fanout-on-write become expensive for a news feed system?
fields.Back: Every post triggers up to 300 fanout writes (one per friend's feed), so total fanout write volume = posts/day × average friend count, which can be orders of magnitude larger than the raw post-write volume.

fields.Front: Estimate storage for 100M posts/day retained for 2 years at ~1KB metadata per post.
fields.Back: 100M × 730 days × 1KB ≈ 73 TB of post metadata over 2 years.

fields.Front: Write the REST endpoint to create a new feed post.
Write the REST endpoint to fetch a user's ranked news feed.
Write a minimal schema for a feed_items table storing a precomputed per-user feed.
fields.Back:
feed_items(
  user_id     BIGINT,
  post_id     BIGINT,
  rank_score  DOUBLE,
  inserted_at TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id)
)

fields.Front: Why store a rank_score alongside each feed item rather than always ranking purely by recency?
fields.Back: It lets the feed service sort by relevance (predicted engagement) instead of just chronological order, and allows re-sorting without recomputing the score from scratch on every read.

fields.Front: Where does ranking typically happen — at fanout/write time, at read time, or both?
fields.Back: Both: an initial score can be computed at fanout time for pre-ranking, but feeds are often re-ranked at read time with fresh signals (recent engagement, freshness decay) before being returned to the user.

fields.Front: How does the celebrity/high-degree-node problem apply to a news feed system beyond just followers?
fields.Back: A single post from a page or user with millions of followers triggers a huge fanout burst; symmetrically, a user who follows an unusually large number of entities makes fanout-on-read expensive too, since their feed read must pull and rank from many sources.

fields.Front: What is the standard hybrid fix for the celebrity problem in a news feed system?
fields.Back: Push (fanout-on-write) for normal accounts with modest follower counts, and pull (fanout-on-read) for high-follower accounts — merging the precomputed feed with a live query against celebrity posts at read time.

fields.Front: Why is ranking (not just fanout mechanism) a distinguishing deep-dive topic for news feed vs. a simple chronological timeline?
fields.Back: A news feed's core value is surfacing the most relevant content, not just the newest, so the system needs a ranking/scoring model (using signals like affinity, engagement rate, recency decay) layered on top of whichever fanout strategy is used.

fields.Front: How does sharding the social graph service help scale a news feed system?
fields.Back: Friend/follow lookups (needed for fanout and feed assembly) are extremely frequent; sharding the graph store (e.g. by user_id) spreads this load across many nodes instead of bottlenecking on one graph database.

fields.Front: What is the tradeoff of caching precomputed feeds in Redis vs. always computing feeds fresh from the database?
fields.Back: Caching gives much faster reads and lower DB load, but risks showing slightly stale content and requires cache invalidation/update logic whenever new posts or engagement signals arrive.

fields.Front: Why might a news feed system accept a ranking model that is 'good enough' rather than a fully real-time ML re-rank on every request?
fields.Back: Full real-time ML inference on every feed load for every candidate post would add significant latency and compute cost; a precomputed/cached approximate ranking, refreshed periodically, is a pragmatic tradeoff between relevance quality and system performance.
New posts are immediately pushed into the precomputed feed_items list of every friend/follower at post time, so feed reads are fast lookups.
A user's feed is assembled at read time by pulling recent posts from all friends/followed entities and ranking them on the fly, so writes stay cheap but reads are more expensive.
